name: Kingfish Limited
sector: Listed Investment Company / NZ Equities Fund
overview: Kingfish Limited is a closed-end listed investment company (LIC) on the NZX Main Board (listed 31 March 2004) that holds a concentrated portfolio of quality, growing New Zealand companies, both listed and unlisted. It is externally managed by Fisher Funds Management Limited under the 'STEEPP' quality-growth investment process. At 31 March 2026 the company held total assets of $432.1m, almost entirely (98%) invested in equities ($422.1m), funded solely by equity (zero debt) with $431.4m of net assets.

business_model.summary: Kingfish earns no operating revenue; it generates 'income' from dividends received on portfolio holdings, interest on cash, and (the dominant swing factor) unrealised/realised changes in the fair value of its investment portfolio. FY2026: dividend and interest income $10.5m, net investment losses -$18.9m, operating expenses and tax -$5.3m, net loss -$13.6m. The company pays shareholders a fixed quarterly cash distribution equal to 2% of average NAV (~8%/year), funded from a mix of income, capital gains and, when those are insufficient, return of capital -- FY2026 dividends paid ($38.1m) far exceeded both dividend income ($10.1m) and the net result (a $13.6m loss), meaning the distribution mechanically eroded NAV per share this year.

revenue_streams.name: Net change in fair value of investments (realised + unrealised)
revenue_streams.note: -$18.9m FY2026 vs prior year strongly positive; this line dominates the P&L swing

business_model.customer_type: Retail and wholesale NZ investors buying listed LIC shares (not B2B/B2C in the operating sense)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand-domiciled underlying investments (NZX-listed and select unlisted NZ companies)

main_competitors: Barramundi Limited (BRM.NZ) -- sister Fisher Funds LIC, Australasian growth focus
Marlin Global Limited (MLN.NZ) -- sister Fisher Funds LIC, international equities
Direct NZX50 index funds/ETFs (e.g. Smartshares NZ Top 50 (FNZ), Kernel NZ 20)
Milford Asset Management (unlisted/KiwiSaver active NZ equity funds)
Fisher Funds' own unit trust equivalents (e.g. Premium New Zealand Fund)
Direct retail stock-picking / other NZ-focused managed funds
competitive_position.market_position: One of a small number of NZX-listed closed-end vehicles giving retail investors packaged exposure to concentrated NZ growth equities, including limited access to unlisted names; sub-scale relative to global LIC peers and increasingly competing against near-zero-fee passive NZX50 index products.

moat_factors.factor: Access to unlisted NZ growth companies
moat_factors.description: Portfolio can include unlisted holdings retail investors otherwise cannot access, but current portfolio (per FY2026 top 10) is overwhelmingly listed large/mid caps
22-year listed history and Fisher Funds brand recognition in NZ retail investment community
PIE tax treatment and one-ticket diversified NZ exposure, but replicable cheaply via index funds
No lock-in; shares trade freely on NZX and can be sold/switched into an index fund at any time

weaknesses: No durable competitive moat versus low-cost NZX50 index ETFs, which have negligible fees versus Kingfish's management/performance fee structure
Concentrated, small/mid-cap NZ-only mandate with limited liquidity in the underlying market
Persistent NAV erosion driven by a distribution policy that is frequently uncovered by earnings
Structural share dilution via warrants (struck near/below NAV) and a discounted (3%) Dividend Reinvestment Plan
Closed-end structure means share price can and does trade at a discount to NAV, an additional structural drag for sellers

growth_drivers: Potential re-rating of the NZ small/mid-cap market from cyclically depressed levels (NZ economy only beginning to recover as of FY2026)

Portfolio companies' own earnings growth (e.g. Fisher & Paykel Healthcare margin expansion, Infratil's CDC Data Centres AI-driven demand, Mercury's generation build-out, Contact Energy's Contact31+ growth plan)
Active share buyback programme (up to 5% of shares on issue) when the share price trades at a meaningful discount to NAV, which is modestly NAV-accretive
Management fee rebate mechanism reduces fee drag automatically when performance is weak (FY2026 fee cut from 1.25% to 0.85% of adjusted NAV, saving $1.9m), partially cushioning bad years
High shareholder appetite for the discounted (3%) Dividend Reinvestment Plan (38% participation) supports steady demand for new shares
Continued NZ interest rate cuts feeding through to household spending power, a tailwind for domestically-exposed holdings (Mainfreight, Vulcan Steel, Freightways, Summerset)

business.description: Top 5 holdings (F&P Healthcare 19%, Infratil 17%, Mainfreight 8%, Summerset 8%, Auckland Airport 8%) are ~60% of the portfolio; company-specific shocks in any one name materially move NAV
Entire mandate is NZX-listed/unlisted NZ companies, a market with limited breadth, depth and liquidity relative to global peers
FY2026 gross performance return of -2.1% badly lagged the S&P/NZX50G's +5.2%, driven by underperforming positions in Vista (-55%), EBOS (-39%), Vulcan Steel (-27%) and Summerset (-19%)

financial.description: NAV/share has fallen from $1.57 (FY2019) to $1.20 (FY2026), a -3.8%/yr decline over 7 years, despite total net assets rising -- the distribution policy (2% of average NAV per quarter, ~8%/yr) is not covered by dividend income or total returns in most years and functions substantially as return of capital

Shares on issue have grown 81% since FY2019 (197.9m to 358.8m) largely via warrant exercises struck near/below NAV and a DRP offered at a 3% discount to market price, diluting existing holders' per-share NAV
Share price traded at times more than a 6% discount to adjusted NAV during FY2026; a widening discount is an additional loss for sellers on top of any NAV decline

regulatory.description: Any adverse change to NZ's Portfolio Investment Entity tax treatment for LICs would reduce the vehicle's relative tax efficiency

NZ government narrowed CRD mandatory reporting scope in Oct 2025; Kingfish ceased to be a climate reporting entity from 2026 -- a modest compliance-cost relief, not a risk, but signals regulatory flux

macro.description: NZ economy showed only tentative recovery through FY2026 before the March 2026 Middle East conflict / Strait of Hormuz closure drove higher fuel prices and interest-rate uncertainty, hitting cyclical holdings (Mainfreight, Vulcan Steel) and rate-sensitive names (Summerset)
Both the discount rate applied to growth-company valuations and NZ mortgage-linked consumer spending (affecting retail/housing-exposed holdings) are sensitive to RBNZ rate moves
US tariff policy (NZ rate raised 10%→15% in FY2026) and broader geopolitical shocks flow through to small open-economy NZ equity valuations

execution.description: Performance entirely dependent on Fisher Funds' stock-picking; FY2026 underperformance versus benchmark shows this can go materially wrong in a single year
Two new independent directors appointed in the past 12 months (Dan Coman, 1 Oct 2025; Simon Flood, 1 Jun 2026) -- routine renewal, not disruptive, but worth monitoring for continuity

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ equity market (S&P/NZX50G) rose 5.2% in the year to March 2026 and reached all-time highs by late 2025 on falling mortgage rates and improving consumer spending power, before a March 2026 Middle East-driven oil price shock reintroduced uncertainty; NZ closed-end LIC sector overall is small and has faced structural headwinds from the rise of low-cost index investing
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high -- NAV and share price directly track NZ (and to a lesser extent Australian) equity market cycles across cyclical exposures (freight, retirement villages, building materials) and defensive exposures (utilities, healthcare)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high -- falling NZ interest rates support portfolio company valuations and consumer-facing holdings (Summerset, retail-adjacent names); rising rates are a headwind to both equity valuations and mortgage-sensitive holdings
key_input_costs: Not directly applicable (investment company); portfolio companies collectively exposed to fuel/energy costs, interest rates, and NZD/USD, NZD/AUD exchange rates

recent_developments.event: Annual shareholders' meeting held (Ellerslie Event Centre, Auckland) following FY2026 annual report release
FY2026 Annual Report released: net loss -$13.6m (FY2025: +$40.8m profit), adjusted NAV return -3.2%, NAV per share fell to $1.20 from $1.35
Simon Flood appointed as new independent director

Exercise date for KFLWI warrant series (allotted 1 May 2025, one warrant per four shares); final exercise price set at $1.24 (reduced from initial $1.35 strike via dividend adjustments totalling 10.84 cps); only 1.40% of the 86.96m warrants on issue were exercised, with the remaining ~85.7m lapsing -- reflecting the share price trading close to/below the strike
Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure triggered a sharp NZ market and portfolio drawdown (NZX50 -5.8% in March 2026), swinging Kingfish's FY26 result from profit to loss
Dan Coman appointed to the Kingfish board
NZ Government announced narrowing of mandatory Climate-related Disclosures regime; Kingfish (sub-$1bn market cap) ceases to be a Climate Reporting Entity from 2026

Management fee automatically stepped down from 1.25% to 0.85% of adjusted NAV under the fee-rebate formula because gross portfolio performance trailed the 90-day bank bill index, saving shareholders $1.9m in fees
Share buyback programme repurchased 0.7m shares (FY2025: 4.8m) while the share price traded at times more than 6% below adjusted NAV

items.target: 2.0% of average NAV per quarter (~8% annualised)
items.notes: Next dividend confirmed at 2.49 cps, payable 26 June 2026, record date 4 June 2026. Policy has been held constant for years despite NAV/share decline -- no formal EPS, revenue or margin guidance is provided as Kingfish is an investment company, not an operating business

items.target: Floating between 0.75% and 1.25% of adjusted NAV depending on performance vs 90-day bank bill index
items.notes: FY2026 rate was 0.85% after the rebate; performance fee (10% of returns above NZ 90-day bank bill + 7% hurdle, subject to a high-water mark, currently $1.15, and capped at 1.25% of adjusted NAV) was not payable in FY2026 given the net loss

items.target: Up to 5% of shares on issue
items.notes: Discretionary, used opportunistically when the share price trades at a meaningful discount to adjusted NAV; repurchased shares are held as treasury stock and recycled through the DRP

guidance.management_commentary: The Chair called FY2026 'disappointing' with a net loss of $13.6m and adjusted NAV return of -3.2%, driven by the portfolio's gross performance return of -2.1% badly lagging the S&P/NZX50G's +5.2%. The Manager (Fisher Funds) stated it 'remains confident in the Manager's investment strategy to focus on well-managed, quality businesses' and does not believe the underperformance in Mainfreight, Vulcan Steel and Summerset reflects company-specific issues, viewing it instead as cyclical/sentiment-driven. No explicit forward return or NAV target was given; management characterised current valuations as attractive for 'patient, long-term investors' given more favourable entry points after the FY2026 drawdown.

nav_per_share.value: $1.20 (statutory NAV, 31 Mar 2026); $1.2977 (undiluted, most recent weekly disclosure, 29 Jul 2026)
nav_per_share.trend: Declining -- $1.57 (FY2019) to $1.20 (FY2026), a -3.8%/yr CAGR over 7 years, primarily due to an uncovered distribution policy and share issuance below NAV
nav_per_share.note: 'Adjusted NAV' (non-GAAP, which adds back cumulative dividends paid) was $6.94 at 31 Mar 2026, used by management to show underlying performance excluding capital return; statutory (as-reported) NAV per share is the relevant number for an investor comparing to the traded share price

discount_premium_to_nav.value: Approximately 1.0% discount to (adjusted) NAV at 31 Mar 2026 (share price $1.19 vs adjusted NAV context); traded at a discount exceeding 6% at times during FY2026; most recent weekly data point (31 May 2026) showed a ~2% discount ($1.24 price vs $1.2702 NAV)
discount_premium_to_nav.trend: Volatile -- swung from an 11.6% PREMIUM to NAV at FY2022 to discounts of 5-6.5% in FY2023-25 and back to roughly 1-2% discount currently
discount_premium_to_nav.note: Historical range shows the discount/premium is highly regime-dependent; buybacks are used tactically when the discount widens materially

adjusted_nav_return.trend: Volatile / recently negative -- FY2022 -3.5%, FY2023 -3.6%, FY2024 +4.6%, FY2025 +8.9%, FY2026 -3.2%; 5-year annualised +0.5%
adjusted_nav_return.note: This is management's preferred underlying-performance metric (adjusts for dividends paid); on this measure Kingfish has barely broken even over 5 years after fees

dividend_yield.value: ~8.4% (FY2026 dividend return, dividends paid ÷ average share price); 10.84 cps paid in FY2026 vs a ~$1.19-1.28 share price range
dividend_yield.trend: Consistently 7.4%-8.6% over the past 5 years, mechanically driven by the fixed 2%-of-average-NAV-per-quarter policy rather than by earnings coverage
dividend_yield.note: High yield is substantially return of capital, not sustainable income -- FY2026 dividends paid ($38.1m) exceeded both dividend income received ($10.1m) and the net result (a $13.6m loss)

shares_on_issue.trend: Up 81% since FY2019 (197.9m), growing every year via warrant exercises and DRP issuance, partially offset by small buybacks
shares_on_issue.note: Continuous net share issuance below/near NAV is a structural dilution risk noted as the central bear-case driver

management_expense_ratio.trend: Declining recently due to the automatic fee-rebate mechanism (management fee cut from 1.25% to 0.85% of adjusted NAV in FY2026 because performance trailed the bank bill index)
management_expense_ratio.note: Structurally far higher than a passive NZX50 index fund (typically <0.5-0.75% and often under 0.3% for the cheapest ETFs), a persistent drag versus the simplest alternative

bull_case: Trades close to NAV currently (roughly 1-2% discount as at mid-2026), removing the 'double discount' risk that has hurt returns in prior years and offering reasonable value if the discount stays contained or closes further

High, consistent quarterly cash distribution (~8% of NAV annualised) appeals to income-seeking investors even though part is return of capital, and the discounted DRP lets long-term holders compound at a slight discount

Concentrated exposure to high-quality NZ growth franchises (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Infratil/CDC data centres, Mercury, Contact Energy, Auckland Airport) that management argues remain fundamentally sound despite a weak FY2026 share price year, with several names guiding to multi-year earnings growth (Mercury underlying earnings to grow ~30% over 5 years, Contact EBITDAF to $1.2-1.3bn, Infratil's CDC benefiting from AI-driven data centre demand)

Automatic fee-rebate mechanism aligns manager incentives with performance and reduced the effective fee load in the recent weak year (1.25% down to 0.85%), and no performance fee is paid without clearing a high water mark

Access to a professionally-managed, single-ticket, tax-efficient (PIE) vehicle for NZ small/mid-cap and select unlisted exposure that would be difficult for retail investors to replicate directly, with active buybacks providing some discount-management support
bear_case: NAV per share has fallen from $1.57 (FY2019) to $1.20 (FY2026), a -3.8%/yr decline, because the fixed 8%-of-NAV annual distribution is not covered by portfolio income or total returns in most years -- FY2026 alone paid out $38.1m in dividends against only $10.1m of dividend income and a $13.6m net loss, meaning the 'yield' is substantially an unsustainable return of investors' own capital

Persistent shareholder dilution: shares on issue have grown 81% since FY2019 via warrants issued near/below NAV and a DRP offered at a 3% discount to market price, both of which transfer value from non-participating to participating/exercising shareholders and structurally cap per-share NAV growth even when the underlying portfolio performs

Fee drag on a sub-scale, single-country equity mandate: even after the FY2026 rebate to 0.85%, the OPEX ratio (1.1%) is several multiples the cost of a passive NZX50 index fund, and a 10% performance fee above a high hurdle plus base fees compounds against investors over time

Concentrated, illiquid exposure to one small equity market: top 5 holdings are ~60% of the portfolio, and FY2026 gross performance (-2.1%) badly lagged the S&P/NZX50G benchmark (+5.2%), showing single-year manager underperformance risk on top of NZ market-specific cyclicality (tariffs, Middle East oil shock, interest rates)

An investor seeking NZ equity exposure could buy a low-cost NZX50 index ETF at a fraction of Kingfish's fee load and without warrant/DRP dilution risk or discount-to-NAV volatility, raising the question of what durable value the LIC wrapper and active management add net of costs, particularly given the 5-year adjusted NAV return of only +0.5% p.a.
